Israeli President Isaac Herzog has officially awarded the mandate to form the next government to Yashar opposition party leader Gadi Eisenkot following the October 27 parliamentary elections. "I am handing over the mandate to form a government to you and wish you every success," Herzog told Eisenkot in a ceremony that was broadcast by the office of the Israeli head of state. "Israel needs a stable government that will be able to work for a long time," the president said and called the political forces represented in parliament to get consolidated. "IT’s time to do everything possible for the sake of unity," he stressed. Eisenkot, for his part, stated that he "hopes to complete the process of forming a government as soon as possible." "We will all have to make compromises. I am glad that my partners understand the importance of this moment and fully support me," he added. Under Israel’s laws, after receiving the mandate, Eisenkot will have 28 days to secure the support of a majority of the members of the 120-seat Knesset (parliament) and form a ruling coalition. If he fails to do so within this time limit, this period may be extended by 14 days more. If the candidate fails, the president will task another lawmaker with forming a government. The second candidate will have two weeks to do so, with no possibility of an extension. If no government can be formed with the support of at least 61 members of parliament, a new election will be called within

headlines.full_text: Off the Charts newsletter: A post mortem of our election model Dan Rosenheck, our data editor, considers why our election forecast missed the signs of the tsunami Republicans weren’t the only losers in America’s midterm elections this week. Spare a tear for The Economist’s congressional model, which was the most conservative of all public forecasts on the expected size of the Democratic wave. Our final predictions gave the party only a 52% chance of winning the Senate, compared with 65-85% for most competitors. And although we did assign a respectable 8% chance to the possibility of Democrats claiming at least the 56 Senate seats they are now expected to have won, there is no such solace for our House forecast. Democrats are on track to secure 260 seats in the lower chamber, one more than the top of our 95% prediction interval.What went wrong? Our model takes a fundamentally different approach to other congressional forecasts, which is why it differs sharply from the consensus. Other models are generally “bottom-up”, which means that they first try to predict the result of each legislative contest, and subsequently estimate the national popular vote as a byproduct of their seat-level forecasts. This approach relies on an assumption that most forecasters take as gospel: polling errors are inevitable, but neither their direction nor their size can be predicted.In contrast, our “top-down” method arrogantly rejects this axiom. Tuesday’s election results handed Democrats the strongest check yet on President Trump’s bid to control the Federal Reserve, by giving them the power to block any allies he might seek to install on its board. That leaves Trump with the chairman of his choosing, Kevin Warsh, but one seat short of a majority and diminished prospects of getting it. His White House has mounted the most direct challenge to the Fed’s independence in decades, including an unprecedented attempt to fire a sitting governor. headlines.full_text: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years The national mood is low, and faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the major parties at the polls. New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather. "It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread." "Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits. "I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further. "Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned. But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower. More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse. Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions. A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere. Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate. headlines.full_text: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte". The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe. The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago. But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access. He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt. Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had athree-month spellas French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member. But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members. He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms". "There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market." Since becoming prime

headlines.full_text: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people. European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week. Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF. The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century. It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January. Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid. The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart. The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries. headlines.full_text: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat While some believe the site should be partially or completely rebuilt, others want it abandoned and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten. Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past. Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era. Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten. But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right. Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU). But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place. Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant. headlines.full_text: Ebola: Why is there still no vaccine? Ebola has been known about for decades, but there is still no vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus causing the current outbreak. New research raises hopes of protection against the various types of Ebola. 1976: A hitherto unknown disease breaks out near the Ebola river in the country then known as Zaire, now theDemocratic Republic of Congo(DRC). This was the first scientifically documentedEbolaepidemic. Now, 50 years on, the DRC once again finds itself at thecenter of a major Ebola outbreak. This time the pathogen is the less common Bundibugyo type of the genus orthoebolavirus. The virus was identified in 2007 during an outbreak in Bundibugyo,Uganda. Another outbreak occurred in the DRC in 2012. How can a virus that has been known for decades continue to infect thousands of people, yet there is still no licensedvaccineor official treatment? Torsten Feldt, a doctor of tropical medicine at Düsseldorf's University Hospital, sees this as a missed opportunity. "We had come across the Bundibugyo virus in two previous outbreaks: 2007 inUgandaand 2012 in DR Congo. So we had enough time to develop vaccines and therapeutic options. But we didn't make use of this opportunity, meaning crucial time was lost during the current outbreak," he said. Leonie Mayer from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Institute for Infection Research and Vaccine Development at the University Medical Center in Hamburg-Eppendorf agrees. "They could of course have developed a vaccine and run pre-clinical trials before," Mayer told DW. headlines.full_text: Should AI companies pay for the journalism they use? Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on? Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events. A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences. Explaining what is happening in the world, why it matters and what it means has traditionally been the work of journalism. Media organizations send reporters into the field, commission investigations and conduct research, producing stories that help audiences understand global events. But as more people turn to AI tools for information, the relationship between those producing journalism and those distributing it is changing. "In the past, search engines likeGoogleindexed our websites and directed users to their articles, generating traffic in return," Julia Becker, publisher of Funke Media Group, told a panel at theGlobal Media Forum (GMF)in Berlin on November 5. "But now that exchange has broken down." "AI companies draw on our quality reporting to generate answers, yet the reporting itself often remains largely invisible by the end of this process," said DW Director General Barbara Massing in a keynote address at the forum. Their remarks reflect a worry that is growing across the media industry. She also said that “two more power lines to Romania are on the way”. European Commissioner for Energy Marta Kos, who was at the ceremony, said Moldova could now “buy energy where it is cheapest”. The 400-kilowatt extra-high-voltage line, which runs from the city of Vulcanesti to Chisinau, allows Moldova to cut reliance on the Cuciurgan thermal power plant in Transnistria. “Every time Moldova dares to choose something other than what Moscow wants, they threaten to cut our electricity,” said Sandu. Africa Watch Copied South Africa’s access to one of its most important export markets is facing fresh uncertainty as Washington moves towards removing the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA). For more than two decades, the trade programme has allowed eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the United States duty-free. South African businesses have used that access to expand operations, reach new customers and create jobs. But a possible withdrawal could change the economics of exporting, leaving companies to reconsider their strategies and the markets they depend on. In this Africa Watch episode, Julie Scheier tells us what is at stake for companies that have invested in meeting American demand, as well as the workers whose livelihoods depend on those exports. The curfew applies to those ranked below sergeant, while higher-ranking service members are exempt. The original 30-day curfew was imposed on all US military personnel in Okinawa on October 9, following the arrest of US serviceman Devin Ballard. He was indicted on charges of robbing and murdering a local woman in Naha, Okinawa Prefecture, earlier that month. Under the rules, troops are barred from leaving bases between midnight and 5 a.m. However, the curfew was breached on October 31 when a US Marine was arrested in Okinawa City on suspicion of drunk driving. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said on Monday that he had urged the US side to strictly enforce military discipline, take effective measures to prevent similar incidents and ensure that the curfew was strictly observed. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi added on Friday that both governments had agreed to strengthen education and training for US service members to prevent further incidents. That led consumers to pull back in spending at department stores and on durable goods, such as appliances and furniture. Spending at general merchandise stores fell 3% in March from the prior month and spending at gas stations declined 5.5% during the same period. Lake Powell, the second-largest human-made reservoir in the US, has lost nearly 7% of its potential storage capacity since 1963, when Glen Canyon Dam was built, a new report shows. In addition to water loss due to anintense multiyear drought, the US Geological Survey and the Bureau of Reclamationreport found, Lake Powell faced an average annual loss in storage capacity of about 33,270 acre-feet, or 11 billion gallons, per year between 1963 and 2018. That’s enough water to fill the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall about 1,600 times. The capacity of the reservoir is shrinking because of sediments flowing in from theColorado and San Juan rivers, according to the report. Those sediments settle at the bottom of the reservoir and decrease the total amount of water the reservoir can hold. As of Monday, Lake Powell was around 25% full, according to data from the Bureau of Reclamation. It’s bad news for a region already facing water shortages and extreme wildfires due to the drought. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration drought experts said last week these conditions areexpected to at least continue– if not worsen – in the coming months. headlines.full_text: Homes and temples glow across India to mark Diwali Millions of Indians are marking the festival of lights with glowing lamps, fireworks and traditional sweets. Millions across India are celebratingDiwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness. The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky. Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers. But the celebrations come amid growingconcerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India. Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse. Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful. India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks. headlines.full_text: Drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield The strike leaves more than 70 percent of northern Iraq's Kurdish region without power. Save Share A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials. The Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power. It was not clear who was responsible for the attack or whether it was related to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad has verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in the Sulaimaniyah governorate. Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Electricity, said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in the cities of Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported. The strike knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of electricity generation off the grid, he said. He added that the ministry would provide electricity to critical facilities, such as hospitals and water treatment plants, by operating hydroelectric power stations and other plants that run on alternative fuel. Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying the explosive-laden drone struck the Khor Mor gas storage facility, reducing the energy grid’s capacity by 70 to 80 percent. headlines.full_text: Mexican mayor found alive after hours-long abduction Rio Bravo mayor freed by captors after being abducted in Zacatecas state, known for cartel-linked violence. Federal officials said Miguel Angel Almaraz was released by his captors on Sunday, hours after being taken to the city of Zacatecas. He was abducted while travelling with family and friends in a region that straddles the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosi on Saturday, when his car was intercepted by armed men, who let the others go. Almaraz’s relatives were able to reach a town in San Luis Potosi, where they alerted authorities about the incident, according to the state’s Security Department. Almaraz is the mayor of Rio Bravo, a municipality of about 110,000 people in Tamaulipas state, 11km (7 miles) from Mexico’s border with Texas, United States. He was acquitted of money laundering charges in 2015, after being imprisoned for six years. He is a member of the conservative National Action Party, but was previously associated with the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution. It is unclear why Almaraz was taken. Authorities say they are investigating the case, including who might be involved in the abduction. Zacatecas state is known for activity involving the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Sinaloa Cartel, both accused of attacking civilians and politicians. headlines.full_text: Iran’s SNSC ratifies agreement with Russia on Rasht–Astara railway TEHRAN – Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) has ratified the agreement with Russia on the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway, clearing the way for accelerated implementation of the strategic infrastructure project, a senior Iranian official announced. TEHRAN – Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) has ratified the agreement with Russia on the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway, clearing the way for accelerated implementation of the strategic infrastructure project, a senior Iranian official announced. Hooshang Bazvand, deputy minister of roads and urban development, told Tasnim News Agency on Sunday that the agreement required approval either by the Iranian Parliament or the SNSC. He said Russia had initially requested that Iran obtain parliamentary approval for the agreement, in line with the procedure followed in Russia. However, following consultations and subsequent efforts, the SNSC approved the agreement last week. Bazvand said the council’s approval would allow the project to move forward at a faster pace. He added that the remaining 37 kilometers of land along the railway route had been handed over to the Russian contractor last Wednesday, bringing the entire 162-kilometer route under the project's disposal for the necessary surveys, technical studies and field assessments. The Rasht–Astara railway is a key missing link in completing the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a major multimodal network designed to connect Russia and other countries in northern Eurasia with Iran and markets further south. He stressed the need to carefully manage foreign exchange resources, saying that despite revenue limitations and difficult conditions for oil and non-oil exports, the central bank had prioritized imports of essential goods by anticipating domestic needs and managing available resources. There had been no shortages of essential goods in the domestic market so far, while the supply of production inputs and medicines would continue, he added. TEHRAN – Central Bank of Iran (CBI) has pledged to provide an additional 400 trillion rials ($800 million) in loans to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), Industry, Mining and Trade Minister Seyed Mohammad Atabak said on Saturday. Speaking at a meeting with entrepreneurs and business representatives in Ardabil Province, Atabak said a support package introduced in December 2025 had initially been designed to assist SMEs. However, assessments showed that a significant portion of the loans had instead gone to large companies. As a result, the Central Bank of Iran has committed to allocating an additional 400 trillion rials specifically to small and medium-sized businesses, he said. Atabak also pointed to the country's foreign currency constraints, saying they had affected some trade policies. Encouraging producers to expand exports and introducing appropriate incentives would help generate more foreign currency earnings, while restrictive export regulations could undermine shipments and foreign currency revenues, he added. headlines.full_text: Serbia's Parliament to meet on Nov 17 after student-led movement won election over strongman Vucic The Students' List won 140 seats in the 250-member assembly while the Serbian Progressive Party won 103. The first session of Serbia's new Parliament, which will be dominated by a student-led movement following its election triumph last month, will be held on Nov. 17, the outgoing parliament speaker said on Sunday. Ana Brnabic scheduled the inaugural parliamentary meeting after Serbia's election authorities last week declared the final results of the Oct. 25 vote. The Students' List won 140 seats in the 250-member assembly while the Serbian Progressive Party won 103, according to those results. The remaining seats go to the parties of ethnic minorities in Serbia. The students led two years of street protests before they toppled strongman Aleksandar Vucic in the election. Protests erupted in response to a train station canopy collapse that killed 16 people in the country's north in November 2024, which many in Serbia blamed on corruption in state infrastructure projects. The Students' List election candidates included mostly professors, teachers and various other experts in their fields but with hardly any political experience, who will now take up parliamentary seats. The group promised to restore the rule of law and terminate corruption that they said flourished under Vucic. The Parliament will first choose a new speaker and other parliamentary bodies. Then a new government should be formed within 90 days. headlines.full_text: IAEA informed about external power loss at Zaporozhye NPP The ZNPP lost connection to its only remaining external power line, Ferosplavnaya-1, early on Sunday morning, The International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi said VIENNA, November 8. /TASS/. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it has been notified that the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) has once again lost external power. "The Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) has once again lost all off-site power, forcing it to rely on emergency diesel generators for reactor cooling and other essential nuclear safety and security functions," the IAEA quoted its Director General Rafael Grossi as saying on its X page. According to Grossi, the ZNPP lost connection to its only remaining external power line, Ferosplavnaya-1, early on Sunday morning. "It is the 27th such event during the conflict, underlining the continued precarious nuclear safety situation," he noted. "The IAEA team at the ZNPP has been informed that the plant currently has sufficient fuel reserves to operate a limited number of emergency diesel generators for around two weeks.," the IAEA said, adding that Grossi emphasized the importance "of both restoring the ZNPP’s connection to the grid and increasing the amount of diesel fuel reserves available at the site.".

headlines.full_text: At least 22 wounded after 5.5-magnitude earthquake rocks central Japan A strong earthquake rocked central Japan on Sunday, injuring at least 22 people and shattering windows of multiple stores. A strong earthquake rocked central Japan on Sunday, injuring at least 22 people and shattering windows of multiple stores. A strong earthquake rocked central Japan on Sunday, injuring at least 22 people and shattering windows of multiple stores. According to Japan’s Meteorological Agency, the earthquake was of magnitude 5.7 and smaller aftershocks were reported soon after. The strong tremors forced people to flee buildings, with a wide area near Aichi Prefecture affected. The region included the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara, and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu, the Associated Press reported. Footage broadcast on Japanese TV showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets. The injuries included those who fell down the stairs while they were trying to flee from their buildings. According to the country's meteorological department, the earthquake struck at 1:04 am (local time) on Sunday and was located about 40 kilometres (25 miles) below the earth’s surface in Shizuoka Prefecture. The region is far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt in the capital. According to official seismic assessments, the violent shaking was felt in Aichi. According to The Associated Press, the Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. The trains were slowed because sometimes quakes can damage the railway tracks the trains run on.

Her next challenge will be to turn that electoral breakthrough into effective leadership of a city facing persistent social, economic and infrastructure problems. Raman ran as an outsider, without the backing of any of her 14 colleagues on the Los Angeles City Council. She also faced opposition from the police union, tensions with sections of the Jewish community and the united support of the Democratic establishment for incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. Washington:President Donald Trump said Tuesday he was delaying 50% U.S. tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports after the two countries reached a last-minute deal hours before the sanctions were to go into effect. The announcement, which Trump made on his social media platform, buys time for more negotiations and avoids, for now, another strain in already tense relations between the historic allies. “I have paused the 50% Tariffs against Canada, that were scheduled to kick in tomorrow morning for three days, based on the fact that Canada and the U.S.A., subject to the finalisation of documents, have a DEAL!” Trump posted on Truth Social less than two hours before the 12:01 a.m. Wednesday deadline. If they had gone into effect as scheduled at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday, Trump’s import taxes would have hit Canadian products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. But the political impact would likely have been bigger than the economic one. Canada had threatened to retaliate against any new tariffs with levies of its own, aggravating a trade fight between countries that sold each other $880 billion worth of goods and services last year. Canadian officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday night.
